prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

She was in terrible pain the whole day, as she had been for months: a slipped disc, and there is nothing more painful. She herself was a nurse’s aide, also a poet just beginning to make a name for her nom de plume. As with most things in life, it happened when she was changing channels on her television. The lucky man, on the other hand, was smiling for the first time in his life, and it was fake. He was an aspiring philosopher of dubious potential, very serious, but somehow lacking in essential depth. He could have been an adequate undertaker. It was not the first time for either of them. It was a civil service, with no music, few flowers. Still, there was a slow and erratic tide of champagne—corks shot clear into the trees. And flashcubes, instant photos, some blurred and some too revealing, cake slices that aren’t what they were meant to be. The bride slept through much of it, and never did we figure out who was on whose team. I think the groom meant it in the end when he said, “We never thought anyone would come.” We were not the first to arrive, nor the last to leave. Who knows, it may all turn out for the best. And who really cares about such special days, they are not what we live for.

outputs.L1: She had been in terrible pain all day, as she had for months now—a slipped disc, and there is no agony quite like it. By profession she was a nurse's aide, and by aspiration a poet, just beginning to make a name for her nom de plume. As with so many things in life, it happened while she was idly changing channels on the television. The fortunate groom, meanwhile, wore his first smile in memory, though it was entirely feigned. He fancied himself a philosopher of uncertain promise—earnest to a fault, yet somehow wanting in genuine depth. He might have made a passable undertaker instead. Neither of them was new to this. The ceremony itself was civil, unadorned by music, sparse in flowers. And yet a slow, irregular tide of champagne flowed nonetheless—corks sailing clean into the trees. There were flashbulbs and instant photographs, some blurred, others revealing more than intended, and slices of cake that fell short of their symbolic promise. The bride drifted in and out of sleep through much of the proceedings, and to this day none of us could say who belonged to which side of the aisle. I believe the groom spoke honestly when he finally remarked, "We never thought anyone would come." We were neither the first to arrive nor the last to leave. Perhaps, in the end, it will all work out for the best. Though really, who is to say such occasions matter so much—they are hardly what we live for.
outputs.L2: She'd been suffering constant agony for months on end: a herniated disc, among the most excruciating afflictions imaginable. Her day job was as a nursing assistant, though she'd also begun establishing herself as a poet under an assumed name. Like so many pivotal moments, this one arrived while she was simply flipping through television channels. He fancied himself a philosopher-in-training, one whose promise remained questionable; earnest to a fault, yet somehow missing any genuine profundity. Funeral direction might have suited him better. outputs.L3:
For months, she had lived with the kind of pain that reorders a person's priorities—a slipped disc that made even the simplest movements of her work as a nurse's aide feel like small acts of defiance against her own body. And yet, in the hours she could steal from exhaustion, she wrote poetry, publishing under a pen name as though her real self needed protection from the vulnerability of verse. Perhaps it did. There is something particular about pain that either closes a person off from language entirely or opens a door to it they never knew existed; for her, it seemed to be the latter.

The man she married was, by most accounts, an aspiring philosopher—though "aspiring" may have been generous, given how little his ideas had matured beyond a certain shallow cleverness, the kind that impresses at dinner parties but rarely survives closer scrutiny. And yet, on their wedding day, something happened to him that no one, least of all himself, seemed to anticipate: he smiled. Not the practiced half-smile he wore in seminars or the smirk he offered when he thought he'd won an argument, but something genuine, unguarded, entirely new to his face. Strange, then, that this authentic expression should feel, to those watching, somehow rehearsed—as if his body was imitating an emotion it had never actually learned to produce.

The ceremony itself was modest to the point of austerity. It was a civil affair, stripped of music, empty of flowers, held in a room that smelled faintly of old paperwork rather than celebration. And yet, despite this bareness, someone had insisted on the trappings of tradition: champagne was poured, photographs were taken, a cake—small, slightly lopsided—was cut and distributed among the guests. It was as though the couple wanted to prove that ritual could survive even when stripped of its usual ornamentation, that the bones of celebration were enough to hold up the appearance of one.

Through much of this, the bride slept. Not fully, perhaps, but in that heavy, medicated half-consciousness that pain and its remedies often produce. Guests exchanged uncertain glances, unsure whether to speak quietly out of respect or to carry on as though nothing were unusual. It left an odd tension in the room, an uncertainty about who belonged to which side of the affair, who was meant to comfort whom, who held allegiance to the bride's exhaustion versus the groom's strange, new joy. The social choreography of a wedding, usually so instinctive, seemed to collapse under the weight of her sleep.

At some point, the groom turned to the room and said, almost to himself, "We never thought anyone would come." There was no performance in it—only surprise, plain and unguarded, the same quality that had marked his smile earlier. It was, perhaps, the most honest thing said all day.

Looking back on it now, I find myself doubting the importance we assign to such occasions. Weddings, birthdays, the milestones we mark with cake and champagne and photographs—they promise to be turning points, thresholds after which everything changes. But so often, they are only rooms full of tired people, half-asleep or half-smiling, waiting for someone to tell them what comes next. Perhaps that uncertainty is the truest part of any celebration: the quiet suspicion that nothing which follows will feel as significant as we were told it would.
outputs.L4:
The pain in her back had become so constant that Marguerite no longer mentioned it to anyone, not even to herself in the mirror in the mornings when she pressed her knuckles into the base of her spine and breathed through the ache before getting dressed for another shift. She worked as a nurse's aide at Fairview, emptying bedpans and turning patients who could no longer turn themselves, and in the evenings, when her hands stopped shaking from the day's exertions, she wrote poems in a spiral notebook she kept hidden beneath a stack of towels in her closet. The poems were not good. She knew this, in the way one knows uncomfortable truths, but she wrote them anyway, small brittle things about hospital corridors and the particular gray of December skies.

She met Theodore on a Tuesday, though "met" was perhaps too deliberate a word for what happened. She was at her sister's apartment, half-watching a nature documentary about deep-sea creatures, when he arrived to return a ladder he'd borrowed weeks before. He stayed for coffee. He talked, almost immediately and without much prompting, about Kant and the categorical imperative, about a paper he was writing—had been writing, apparently, for several years—on the nature of moral obligation. He used words like "phenomenological" and "ontological" with the ease of a man who had memorized their shapes without necessarily inhabiting their meanings. Marguerite found herself both bored and strangely attentive, the way one might watch a magic trick whose mechanism you suspect but cannot quite name.

They began seeing each other with no particular momentum, meeting for lunch near the hospital, walking through the park where he would gesture at pigeons and make some point about determinism. It was never clear to her when they had decided to marry, only that one day he mentioned a date, a Thursday six weeks out, and she had nodded as though this were the natural continuation of a conversation already underway.

The ceremony took place in a municipal building with fluorescent lighting and the smell of floor wax. There was no music—neither of them had thought to arrange for any, and the clerk, a heavyset woman with reading glasses on a chain, did not seem to expect it either. Theodore wore a gray suit that did not quite fit him in the shoulders. Marguerite wore a blue dress she had bought two years prior for her cousin's funeral, the only formal thing she owned that did not aggravate the pain in her back when she stood for long periods.

Afterward, in the hallway outside the clerk's office, someone—she never determined who, possibly a coworker of Theodore's, possibly a distant relative—produced a bottle of champagne and a stack of paper cups. The cork popped too loudly and startled a woman filing paperwork at a nearby desk. Photographs were taken with someone's phone, blurred and poorly composed, Theodore's eyes closed in nearly every frame, Marguerite's smile arriving a half-second too late or leaving a half-second too early. Her sister cried, though not, Marguerite suspected, from any excess of sentiment but because she had been crying on and off for weeks over an unrelated matter involving her landlord.

No one had brought flowers. No one had reserved a table anywhere for lunch. They stood in the hallway drinking flat champagne from paper cups while a line of people waiting for other business—a parking dispute, a business license—glanced at them with mild curiosity before returning to their phones.

Marguerite watched all this with the same detached attention she brought to her poems, cataloguing details without quite committing to their significance. It occurred to her, standing there in her secondhand blue dress with champagne warming in her hand, that no one present had actually expected there to be guests, had actually planned for witnesses beyond the required two, and that this fact alone seemed to say something true about the day—that despite what people insisted, despite the industries built around anniversaries and the specific weight assigned to certain dates on a calendar, this was not, in fact, what anyone lived for. It was not the accumulation of such days that constituted a life, not the champagne or the badly composed photographs or the dress bought for a funeral now repurposed for a wedding. It was something else, something that happened in the unremarkable hours between such occasions—in the turning of a patient's body at 3 a.m., in the specific ache of a spine that would not stop aching, in a conversation about pigeons that meant nothing and yet had somehow, through no clear mechanism, arrived at this hallway, this champagne, this man with his eyes closed in every photograph.

She finished her champagne. Someone suggested they get lunch, and no one objected, and so they filed out of the building into the gray afternoon, already forgetting, in the particular way people do, that anything of consequence had happened at all.
outputs.L5:
# Still

She walked through the empty house one final time. The rooms, once filled with laughter and the chaos of everyday life, now held only echoes. Still, she lingered by the window where morning light used to spill across the kitchen table.

She remembered the arguments, the celebrations, the quiet Tuesday evenings that meant nothing and everything. The walls had absorbed decades of conversation, and though the furniture was gone, she could still hear fragments—a child's laugh, a door closing, someone calling her name from another room.

Still, she wasn't ready to let go completely.

The movers would arrive tomorrow to take the last boxes. The new owners, a young couple with dreams of their own, would soon fill these spaces with different sounds, different rhythms. She understood this was how it worked—houses didn't belong to people, not really. People simply passed through them, leaving traces that faded like breath on glass.

She touched the doorframe where pencil marks once tracked a child's growing height, now painted over but somehow still visible to her eyes alone. The house had witnessed her entire adult life: her marriage, her children's first steps, the slow accumulation of ordinary days that somehow added up to something extraordinary.

Still, standing in that hollow space, she felt gratitude more than grief. The house had done its job—it had sheltered love, weathered storms, held space for growth and change. Now it would do the same for someone else.

She took one last breath of the familiar air, memorizing the particular quality of light through the western windows. The house would remain standing long after she drove away, still holding its secrets, still waiting for new stories to unfold within its walls.

Some places, she realized, never really leave us. We carry them forward, still present in memory, long after the physical space becomes someone else's beginning.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece of literary fiction about an unconventional wedding, told from the perspective of a guest with a wry, detached tone.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Reception

The bride wore her grandmother's dress, altered to accommodate the tattoo of a koi fish that swam up her spine and, apparently, needed to breathe. The groom wore Crocs. Not ironically, I don't think. Just Crocs, the way some men wear the same brand of underwear their whole lives without examining why.

I'd known Marla since college, back when she cried during phone commercials and alphabetized her spice rack. Now she stood barefoot in a community garden in October, marrying a man named Theo who ran a mushroom foraging business and had once, by his own admission, lived in a van "not as a bit."

The officiant was Marla's aunt, ordained online that morning, reading from a laminated card with the seriousness of someone handling classified documents. She kept calling Theo "Teo," and no one corrected her, which felt like its own kind of vow.

There were no chairs. This was, I gathered, intentional—something about "grounding" and "presence." I stood through forty minutes of ceremony developing what I can only describe as an intimate relationship with my own lower back, while a golden retriever named Kant wandered the aisle wearing a bowtie and total indifference to the proceedings.

The vows included the word "ecosystem" four times. Theo cried discussing compost. I am not being unkind; I counted because I had nothing else to do with my hands, having been asked not to bring my phone, "for the energy."

At the reception—a barn, obviously, strung with the kind of lights that suggest someone's Pinterest board achieving sentience—the cake was vegan and tasted like a candle. The first dance was to a song I didn't recognize, something with a ukulele, and Theo dipped Marla so enthusiastically that her grandmother's dress made a sound like tearing paper, which everyone pretended not to hear.

I found myself next to Marla's mother, who was drinking chardonnay from a mason jar with the grim determination of a woman doing long division in her head.

"They're happy," she said, not quite a question.

"They seem to be," I said, which was true. That was the strange part. Amid the Crocs and the composting and the dog in formalwear, there was something almost violently sincere happening—two people who had built, out of foraged mushrooms and karmic debt and whatever ecosystem metaphors were left, a thing that looked, despite every instinct I had to mock it, like it might actually hold.

Later, I watched Marla laughing at something Theo whispered, her tattoo catching the fairy lights, looking more unguarded than I'd seen her since we were twenty-two and she still believed the world owed her something gentle.

I ate my candle-cake. I toasted with a jar. I thought: ridiculous, and also, damn it, lovely—the two words arriving, as they often do at weddings, entirely without permission.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a surreal, poetic narrative about two mismatched people getting married, blending irony and melancholy.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Wedding of Salt and Paper

They married on a Tuesday, which is to say the calendar barely noticed.

She arrived made entirely of salt—crystalline, precise, prone to dissolving whenever anyone cried near her, which was often, because weddings do that to people. He was paper, folded so many times in his life that he'd forgotten his original shape, only remembering that once, long ago, he had been a single flat sheet with nothing written on him.

The priest was a clock with no hands, which meant the ceremony lasted exactly as long as it needed to and not one second more.

"Do you take this paper," the clock asked, though its mouth was just two numbers meeting at odd angles, "to hold, though holding him means becoming damp, means becoming the thing that unmakes you?"

She said yes. Salt always says yes. It's in her nature to agree until she disappears.

"Do you take this salt," the clock continued, "to contain, though containing her means eventually you'll dissolve too, means your edges will curl and blur and you'll never again be sharp enough to cut a clean line?"

He said yes, because paper is good at holding things it shouldn't, at absorbing what it cannot survive.

The guests were mostly weather. A low-pressure system sat in the front row, weeping intermittently. Autumn leaves had been invited but arrived as their own ghosts, translucent and unable to applaud. Somewhere, a second clock—this one with hands but no face—ticked in 4/4 time, providing the only music, a waltz for people who would rather not dance.

They kissed. Of course they kissed. What else do you do when the universe has arranged you into adjacent shapes and called it love?

Where their mouths met, something happened that wasn't quite chemistry and wasn't quite tragedy but lived in the narrow hallway between the two. She grew softer at the edges. He grew translucent at the center, like a window that had given up pretending to be a wall.

"I don't know how to be dry with you," he whispered, which was the paper way of saying *I don't know how to survive this and I've chosen you anyway.*

"I don't know how to be whole without dissolving a little," she whispered back, which was the salt way of admitting *the only cure for loneliness is the thing that will eventually erase me.*

They cut the cake, which was made of fog and tasted like the last day of childhood—there and then not there, sweet and then only a memory of sweetness.

For the first dance, they moved like two people who understood that every embrace is a small preview of ruin. He held her carefully, the way you hold a thing you know you'll lose. She let herself be held, the way you allow the inevitable to feel, briefly, like tenderness instead of erosion.

Years from now—though time moved strangely at this wedding, doubling back on itself like a paper airplane that refuses to land—someone will find them. Salt-stains on paper, warped and permanent, an artifact of two mismatched elements that tried anyway.

It will look, to whoever finds it, like a map.

It will be illegible. It will be the only proof that they existed at all.

The clock with no hands pronounced them married. The clock with no face kept perfect time. And somewhere in the space between dissolving and curling, between disappearing and remembering, they built something neither of them had words for—

not quite a marriage.

Not quite a wound.

Something that was, stubbornly, both.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a flash fiction story that begins with a woman in pain and ends at a strange civil wedding ceremony.
counterfactuals.output:
**Occlusion**

The pain arrived at 4 a.m. like a fist closing around her skull, and Marguerite lay very still in the dark, breathing through her teeth, waiting for the world to stop tilting. This was the third time this month. The doctor called it a migraine with aura; she called it the white bird, because that's what she saw first—a flickering, feathered shape at the edge of her vision, wings beating against the inside of her eye.

She did not call anyone. There was no one, really, to call. Her mother was three states away and asleep. Her sister didn't pick up before nine. So she lay on the bathroom floor with a cold washcloth pressed to her forehead and negotiated with the pain the way you'd negotiate with a landlord: *just let me function, just let me get through this one thing, and I'll never ask for anything again.*

By ten, the fist had loosened its grip to something more like a hand resting on her head, heavy but no longer crushing. She showered. She put on the green dress because it was the only clean one, and green, she thought, was a reasonable color for a Tuesday.

The county clerk's office smelled like carpet cleaner and stale coffee, fluorescent lights humming a note just below hearing. Frank was already there, sitting on a plastic chair with his hat in his lap like a man at a bus station. They had known each other four months. He fixed water heaters. He liked her because she didn't ask him to talk about his feelings, and she liked him because he made her laugh exactly once a day, no more, no less, as if he'd read somewhere that this was the correct dosage.

They were marrying because his insurance was better than hers, and because the lease on her apartment was up, and because, if she was honest, the alternative was continuing to live alone with a bird that lived behind her eyes.

The officiant was a woman named Dolores with a laminated card and a voice like a recorded announcement. Behind her, taped to the wall, was a poster about fire safety. Two other couples waited on folding chairs, one of them arguing in whispers about parking validation.

"We can begin whenever you're ready," Dolores said, and Frank looked at Marguerite, and Marguerite realized the pain had followed her here—not gone, only diminished, sitting behind her left eye like a coin lodged in a slot machine, waiting to drop.

"I'm ready," she said, because it was true in the specific, narrow way that most true things are.

Dolores read the vows off her card in the same tone she might use to read parking regulations. Somewhere a copier churned out forms. A child in the waiting area cried once, briefly, and was hushed. Frank's hands, when she took them, smelled like solder and coffee, and this steadied her more than she expected.

"Do you take this man," Dolores said, and Marguerite watched, over Dolores's shoulder, a pigeon land on the windowsill outside, gray and ordinary, nothing like the white bird at all, just a city pigeon looking for crumbs, and she thought: *there it is, the actual bird, the one that doesn't live in my skull.*

"I do," she said, and the fist behind her eye, as if satisfied that it had made its point, finally, quietly, let go.

Frank slid a ring onto her finger that he'd bought at a pawn shop and apologized for twice already. Dolores stamped something. The fluorescent lights kept humming. Somewhere down the hall, another couple was announced husband and wife, and a small ragged cheer went up, and Marguerite laughed—her one laugh, early today, but she'd allow it—and outside the window, the pigeon lifted off into the ordinary gray sky, and did not come back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece in the style of a prose poem describing a bride and groom whose backstories don't quite add up, with a cynical narrator.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Wedding of Convenient Fictions**

Here they come, down an aisle strewn with petals that cost more than the flowers they resemble, the bride in white like she invented the color, like no one ever wore it before her and meant it less. The groom waits with his hands folded the way men fold their hands when they're rehearsing sincerity. Watch how he doesn't blink. Practiced men don't blink.

She says she grew up on a lake in Michigan, in a house with a wraparound porch and a father who taught her to fish. But her voice does something strange around the word *lake*—catches, like it's translating from a language she learned last spring. I've seen the photograph she keeps in her clutch, worn soft at the corners like heirlooms are supposed to be worn. It's a stock photo. I'd bet the ceremony hall on it. Some sunset, some pier, some family that belongs to no one, purchased for the frame.

He says Ohio. He says his mother sang in the church choir, that his father built the tool shed with his own two hands, that he was voted Most Likely to Stay. But ask him the name of a single street and he reaches for it like a man reaching for a coat that isn't on the hook anymore. His childhood is a room he's furnished from a catalog. Everything matches. Nothing was chosen.

The officiant asks if there is any reason these two should not be joined, and the silence that follows is the loudest sound in the building — a silence thick with everyone's private arithmetic not adding up, and everyone's polite refusal to show their work.

Look at the rings. Real gold, at least — I'll grant them that. Objects don't lie, only people wearing them. The bride's hand trembles when he slides hers on, and I want to believe it's love, I do, I want it so badly I could write it into the record myself. But trembling is what hands do when they're holding a story together with both fists.

They kiss. The room exhales the way rooms do when they've decided not to ask further questions. Somewhere in the back, a woman who might be an aunt or might be a woman paid to look like one dabs her eyes with a napkin that says *Congratulations* in gold cursive, as if the napkin knows more than we do, as if it printed itself with confidence borrowed from nobody's actual past.

I don't know who these people were before this morning. I don't think they do either. But watch them walk out together into the flashbulbs, into the thrown rice, into the long white car idling like a getaway — and try to tell me that isn't its own kind of truth: two people so sure of the future they didn't bother getting the past exactly right.

Maybe that's the only vow that ever holds. Not *I know you*. Just: *I'll help you carry whatever you're calling your name.*

The car pulls away. The petals are already browning at the edges. Somebody's already vacuuming the aisle, already erasing the evidence, already getting the room ready for the next beautiful, unverifiable thing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short story about a wedding that feels off—awkward guests, a sleepy bride, a fake smile—narrated with dry, philosophical commentary on love and life's "special days."
counterfactuals.output:
# The Special Day

The banquet hall had been rented for its "timeless elegance," which meant it looked like every other banquet hall built after 1994, with gold-flecked wallpaper and a ceiling fan that turned like it, too, had reservations about the whole affair. Someone had lit candles despite the fact that it was two in the afternoon and the sun was doing a perfectly adequate job on its own. This is the nature of special days: we insist on adding light to daylight, as though ordinary illumination were an insult to the occasion.

The bride, whose name was Marissa, sat at the head table with the specific stillness of a woman who had been awake since four a.m. having her hair pulled taut by strangers who kept saying "gorgeous" in the tone people use for weather. Her eyes had the glazed patience of someone waiting out a dental procedure. Every so often she would surface, remember where she was, and produce a smile of such architectural precision—teeth, cheeks, a practiced crinkle near the eyes—that it seemed less an expression of joy than a passport photo of one.

This is, of course, what we mean by "happiest day of your life": a day so encrusted with expectation that actual happiness, if it dares show up, has to elbow its way past the seating chart.

The guests performed the rituals expected of them. An uncle who had not spoken to the bride's father in nine years stood near the punch bowl, laughing at a joke no one had told, technically present, spiritually elsewhere. Two bridesmaids compared shoes with the grim intensity of soldiers comparing wounds. A child under a table narrated his own wedding to an unimpressed stuffed rabbit, getting the vows more right than the actual officiant would.

The officiant—ordained online, three days prior, for the express purpose of this event—cleared his throat and began to speak about love as though he had invented the concept that morning. "Love," he said, "is patient. Love is kind." He did not mention that love is also, frequently, a woman falling asleep during her own vows because she'd stayed up till 2 a.m. hot-gluing centerpieces that would be thrown away by Sunday.

The groom, Tobias, watched her with the expression of a man watching a plane he is fairly sure will land, but has no actual control over. He reached for her hand at the appointed moment and she surfaced again, blinking, delivering the smile—click, click, teeth, crinkle—like a nervous system responding to a stimulus rather than a woman responding to a man.

We like to believe certain days are separated from the ordinary river of days—that a wedding, a funeral, a graduation exists in some higher atmosphere, untouched by the boredom and confusion of a Tuesday. But a wedding is still made of minutes, and minutes do not care what you've named them. They pass identically whether you're falling in love or falling asleep, whether you're a bride or a table centerpiece, quietly wilting under the same relentless clock.

At the reception, someone's speech ran fourteen minutes over and contained the sentence "when Tobias first told me about Marissa, I knew," without ever specifying what, exactly, was known. The DJ played a song about eternal love that had, in fact, been written for a phone commercial. The cake, which had cost more than the officiant's entire online ordination, tasted like damp optimism.

And yet.

At some point past ten, when half the guests had left and the ones remaining had stopped performing joy and simply were—loose-tied, unbuttoned, dancing badly to something with too much bass—Marissa laughed. Not the practiced kind. A real one, sudden, almost embarrassing in its honesty, at something Tobias whispered that no one else heard. For exactly four seconds, the fake smile's architecture collapsed into something unplanned and human.

It's a small thing, four seconds. Hardly worth building a whole mythology of "special days" around. But perhaps that's the quiet joke of it all—that we spend such effort staging the extraordinary, and it arrives anyway, briefly, sideways, when no one's watching for it. The banquet hall didn't notice. The candles kept burning against the useless daylight. The ceiling fan kept turning, unconvinced.

Somewhere under a table, the child finished marrying the stuffed rabbit to a fork, pronounced them happy, and moved on with his life, which seemed, on the whole, the correct amount of ceremony to give the thing.
